clinicalPearls: A painless autoimmune destructive thyroiditis occurring within about a year of delivery (or miscarriage)
It classically follows a triphasic course of thyrotoxicosis, then hypothyroidism, then recovery, though many present with only one phase
It is strongly associated with thyroid peroxidase antibodies detectable before or during pregnancy
The thyrotoxic phase is destructive with low radioactive iodine uptake, distinguishing it from Graves disease
Symptoms are easily mistaken for normal postpartum fatigue or postnatal depression
A significant proportion develop permanent hypothyroidism and it tends to recur after future pregnancies
reference.pathophysiology: Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis unmasked by the immune rebound that follows the relative immunosuppression of pregnancy. Immune-mediated destruction of thyroid follicles releases stored hormone, causing a transient thyrotoxic phase, after which hormone depletion produces hypothyroidism before the gland usually recovers. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies mark the underlying autoimmunity and predict risk. As a destructive process, radioactive iodine uptake is low and antithyroid drugs are unhelpful.
additionalDifferentials: Normal postpartum fatigue or postnatal depression
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests across the phases
Radioactive iodine uptake if Graves disease must be excluded (avoiding breastfeeding considerations)
Follow-up thyroid function to detect permanent hypothyroidism
Screening in subsequent pregnancies given recurrence risk
redFlags: Persistent hypothyroidism affecting the mother and breastfeeding
reference.prognosis: Most women return to euthyroidism within a year, but many develop permanent hypothyroidism over subsequent years, and the condition frequently recurs after later pregnancies.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to normal postpartum tiredness or depression
Treating the thyrotoxic phase with antithyroid drugs
Confusing it with Graves disease and giving radioactive iodine
Not arranging follow-up for permanent hypothyroidism
management: Control symptomatic thyrotoxic-phase adrenergic symptoms with a beta-blocker, since the destructive process does not respond to antithyroid drugs
Treat the hypothyroid phase with levothyroxine replacement when the patient is symptomatic or is planning or continuing pregnancy
Avoid antithyroid drugs and radioactive iodine, distinguishing this destructive thyroiditis from Graves disease by the low radioactive iodine uptake
Monitor thyroid function serially through the triphasic course to guide, and later withdraw, treatment
Undertake long-term follow-up to detect permanent hypothyroidism, which develops in a significant proportion
Screen thyroid function in subsequent pregnancies given the recurrence risk, and check thyroid peroxidase antibodies
